model-opacity-shield.ex_ai: Developers saying they cannot fully explain their systems is used to soften transparency duties, so disclosure is required only where technically feasible.

unit-selection.name: Choice of measurement unit
unit-selection.plain: The unit a law uses to count a harm, such as net totals or averages, can make the same facts look small or large.
unit-selection.check: Find the unit or measure used to count the harm or benefit. Ask whether a different unit, such as gross rather than net or totals rather than averages, would give a different answer, and who chose this one.
unit-selection.fix: State the unit explicitly, or require reporting in more than one unit, including gross and net figures.
unit-selection.ex_ai: The unit a law uses to count harm, such as net jobs or average screen time, can make the same facts look small or large.
unit-selection.ex_other: For illustration: a bill measuring housing loss by the net number of units in a county could show no loss even if affordable units were replaced by luxury ones.

temporal-averaging.name: Averaging over long periods
temporal-averaging.plain: Measuring impact as an average over a year or longer can hide harms that are concentrated in short windows, such as a single season or week.
temporal-averaging.check: Find every period over which impact is measured or reported. Ask whether harm could be concentrated in a short window that a yearly average would hide, and whether peaks are reported separately.
temporal-averaging.fix: Require reporting of peak and short-window figures alongside averages, or set limits that apply to the worst period.
temporal-averaging.ex_ai: Measuring impact as an average across a year or an election cycle hides concentrated harms that occur in short windows.
temporal-averaging.ex_other: For illustration: a bill capping river pollution by an annual average could permit severe spikes in a few weeks of low flow.

threshold-selection.name: Threshold for what counts
threshold-selection.plain: A high or hard to prove threshold for what counts as harm or a violation can leave almost nothing covered, even where the wording sounds protective.
threshold-selection.check: Find the words that set how serious or how proven something must be before the law applies. Ask who must prove it, to what standard, and how many real cases would clear the bar.
threshold-selection.fix: Define the threshold with examples or a measurable test, and place the burden of proof where the information sits.
threshold-selection.ex_ai: A high or hard to prove threshold for what counts as harm or interference, such as materially altered, can leave almost nothing covered.
threshold-selection.ex_other: For illustration: a consumer lending bill covering only practices that cause substantial injury could exclude many small but repeated charges.

who-conducts-assessment.name: Who runs impact assessments
who-conducts-assessment.plain: When the regulated party or its chosen reviewer controls the method and conduct of an assessment, the result can reflect that party's preferences.
who-conducts-assessment.check: Find each required assessment, audit or review. Ask who selects the reviewer, who sets the method, who sees the results, and whether the regulator or an independent party can check them.
who-conducts-assessment.fix: Require independent selection of reviewers, regulator-approved methods, and access to underlying data.
who-conducts-assessment.ex_ai: When the company or its chosen auditor controls the methodology and conduct of an impact assessment, the assessment may reflect the company's preferences.
who-conducts-assessment.ex_other: For illustration: a chemical safety bill could let each plant hire its own consultant and choose the test method for its required risk report.

measurable-vs-matters.name: Easy metrics over important ones
measurable-vs-matters.plain: Duties built around figures that are easy to count can leave out harms that are harder to measure, so reporting looks complete while missing what matters.
measurable-vs-matters.check: Find the quantities a law requires to be counted or reported. Ask whether they are the easiest things to count or the things that track harm, and which real harms have no metric at all.
measurable-vs-matters.fix: Pair countable measures with required qualitative reporting on harms that resist measurement.
measurable-vs-matters.ex_ai: Reporting duties built around easy numbers such as compute or API calls can leave out harder to measure harms such as loss of autonomy.
measurable-vs-matters.ex_other: For illustration: a workplace safety bill might require reporting of hours worked and injuries counted, yet say nothing about chronic stress or near misses.

latency-attribution.name: Proof of causation required first
latency-attribution.plain: Requiring established causal proof before action can delay rules until effects are entrenched, since long term harms often take years to document.
latency-attribution.check: Find language that requires proof, evidence of causation or established findings before a rule, penalty or duty applies. Ask how long such proof usually takes and what happens in the meantime.
latency-attribution.fix: Allow action on credible indicators, with a duty to revisit as evidence develops.
latency-attribution.ex_ai: Requiring established causal proof of harm before action can delay rules until effects are entrenched, since long term harms take years to document.
latency-attribution.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on a new food additive could bar any restriction until studies prove causation of illness, which could take a decade.

new-jobs-assumption.name: Assumed offset for displaced parties
new-jobs-assumption.plain: Methods that assume affected people will quickly find equivalent alternatives can leave out harm where the change is faster or harder than in the past.
new-jobs-assumption.check: Find any estimate or program built on an assumption that affected people will adjust or be replaced elsewhere. Ask what evidence supports the assumption, how fast adjustment must be, and who bears the gap.
new-jobs-assumption.fix: State the assumption, test it against past transitions, and provide support that does not depend on it.
new-jobs-assumption.ex_ai: Methods that assume displaced workers will find new roles leave out harm in cases where transitions are faster or harder than before.
new-jobs-assumption.ex_other: For illustration: a trade bill could count closed factories as offset by projected new service jobs in another region, without counting the gap in time, pay or place.

policy-enforcement-split.name: Policy and enforcement in different bodies
policy-enforcement-split.plain: Assigning rulemaking and enforcement to separate bodies with different standards can let each point to the other when gaps appear.
policy-enforcement-split.check: Find which body writes the rules and which enforces them. Ask whether they share standards, deadlines and data, and who is responsible when a gap falls between them.
policy-enforcement-split.fix: Name one lead body, or require joint standards, shared data and a rule for resolving disputes.
policy-enforcement-split.ex_ai: Assigning rulemaking and enforcement to separate bodies with different standards lets each point to the other when gaps appear.
policy-enforcement-split.ex_other: For illustration: a water quality bill might give one agency the power to set limits and another the power to inspect, with neither required to act when the limits prove unworkable.

platform-model-liability.name: Responsibility unassigned across supply chain
platform-model-liability.plain: If the law does not say which party in a chain of makers, distributors and users is responsible for a harm, no one may be clearly liable.
platform-model-liability.check: Map each party in the chain from maker to end user. Ask which one the law holds responsible for each type of harm, and whether a harm could fall between two parties.
platform-model-liability.fix: Allocate responsibility by stage and harm type, with a default party when roles are disputed.
platform-model-liability.ex_ai: If the law does not say whether model makers, platforms or users are responsible, no party is clearly liable for harmful output.
platform-model-liability.ex_other: For illustration: a product safety bill might separately define manufacturers, importers and sellers of a device but never say who answers for a defect that arises in assembly.

regulatory-arbitrage.name: Coverage tied to where a firm locates
regulatory-arbitrage.plain: Jurisdictional hooks that depend on where a company places its operations or registration let it choose the place with the lightest rules.
regulatory-arbitrage.check: Find what ties an entity to the law, such as where it is established, located or incorporated. Ask whether the entity can change that fact cheaply and whether the law then stops applying.
regulatory-arbitrage.fix: Base coverage on where effects or customers are, not only on where the firm sits.
regulatory-arbitrage.ex_ai: Jurisdictional hooks that depend on where a company locates operations let it choose the place with the lightest rules.
regulatory-arbitrage.ex_other: For illustration: a data breach notice law that applies to firms headquartered in the state could be avoided by moving a headquarters while keeping the same customers.

mutual-recognition.name: Treating foreign rules as equivalent
mutual-recognition.plain: Treating another jurisdiction's weaker rules as equivalent can lower the effective standard for entities that comply there.
mutual-recognition.check: Find any clause that accepts compliance with other rules as satisfying this law. Ask who decides equivalence, by what test, whether it can be reviewed, and whether the other rules are enforced.
mutual-recognition.fix: Define equivalence by a stated test, require periodic review, and allow withdrawal of recognition.
mutual-recognition.ex_ai: Treating weaker foreign regulation as equivalent can lower the effective standard for companies that comply abroad.
mutual-recognition.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on imported medical devices could accept approval by another country as equal to local review, even if that country tests less.

surveillance-laundering.name: Tools reused for a different purpose
surveillance-laundering.plain: Tools built for one authorized purpose, such as defense, can be reused for another, such as domestic policing, and fall outside rules written for the second purpose.
surveillance-laundering.check: Find each purpose or user category the law covers or exempts. Ask what happens when a tool made for one is used for another, and whether the rules follow the use or the original purpose.
surveillance-laundering.fix: Attach rules to the actual use, and require new authorization when a tool changes purpose.
surveillance-laundering.ex_ai: Systems built for military use may be reused for domestic policing and fall outside rules written for civilian products.
surveillance-laundering.ex_other: For illustration: a bill regulating civilian drone cameras might exempt equipment built for the armed forces, even when a city police department later buys it.

revolving-door.name: No cooling-off period
revolving-door.plain: Without a waiting period for officials who move to regulated firms, an agency can become a training ground for industry staff.
revolving-door.check: Check whether the law restricts officials from joining firms they oversee, and firms' staff from joining the agency without recusal. Ask for the length of any wait, what it covers, and who enforces it.
revolving-door.fix: Add a cooling-off period, recusal rules and disclosure of job negotiations for officials.
revolving-door.ex_ai: Without a waiting period for officials moving to regulated firms, the agency can become a training ground for industry staff.
revolving-door.ex_other: For illustration: a bill creating a new banking regulator might say nothing about senior examiners taking jobs at the banks they just examined.

pre-post-deployment.name: Monitoring after release over testing before
pre-post-deployment.plain: Favoring monitoring after release over testing before release leaves harms to be corrected after the fact, which does not help when effects cannot be reversed.
pre-post-deployment.check: Find when each check happens relative to release or use. Ask whether the harm could be reversed once it occurs, and whether the law relies on later monitoring where earlier testing is possible.
pre-post-deployment.fix: Require testing before release for harms that cannot be undone, with monitoring added after.
pre-post-deployment.ex_ai: Favoring monitoring after release over testing before release leaves harms to be corrected after the fact, which does not help when effects cannot be reversed.
pre-post-deployment.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on a new pesticide could rely on post-sale monitoring of soil, which cannot undo contamination found years later.

premature-regulation.name: Always too early to act
premature-regulation.plain: Readiness reviews or short reauthorization windows can make the right time to regulate always later, since fields keep changing.
premature-regulation.check: Find any review, readiness test or renewal that must happen before a rule applies. Ask who decides when conditions are met, whether there is a deadline, and whether the answer can be no indefinitely.
premature-regulation.fix: Set firm dates for action and require reviews to end in a decision.
premature-regulation.ex_ai: Readiness reviews or short reauthorization windows can make the right time to regulate always later, since technology keeps changing.
premature-regulation.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on autonomous farm equipment safety might wait until a council finds the field mature, with no date for that finding.

let-market-correct.name: Waiting period for voluntary solutions
let-market-correct.plain: Requiring voluntary or market-based solutions to be tried first builds in a waiting period while harm continues, and what counts as insufficient is rarely defined.
let-market-correct.check: Find any step that must come before a mandatory rule, such as voluntary measures or industry action. Ask who judges success, by what test, and how long the wait can last.
let-market-correct.fix: Define a measurable test and a deadline after which mandatory rules apply.
let-market-correct.ex_ai: Requiring market-based or voluntary solutions to be tried first builds in a waiting period while harm continues, and insufficient is rarely defined.
let-market-correct.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on packaging waste might require agencies to wait for industry recycling pledges to fail before setting any binding target.

no-maintenance-duty.name: No duty after release
no-maintenance-duty.plain: Without ongoing duties, a maker can sell or release a product and leave it in use without updates or support, even while it keeps serving important functions.
no-maintenance-duty.check: Look for duties that continue after sale or release, such as support, repair, patching or notice of defects. Ask who is responsible for year five and what happens if the maker exits.
no-maintenance-duty.fix: Require a stated support period, notice before support ends, and a duty to fix known defects.
no-maintenance-duty.ex_ai: Without ongoing duties, companies can release systems and leave them in use without updates or support while they keep making consequential decisions.
no-maintenance-duty.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on connected medical implants might regulate approval but not require the maker to patch security flaws after a few years.

model-update-loophole.name: Approval does not cover later changes
model-update-loophole.plain: If minor changes do not require new review, an approved thing can change substantially over time without fresh evaluation.
model-update-loophole.check: Find the trigger for re-review, such as material or substantial change. Ask who decides whether a change meets it, whether small changes can add up, and whether the approved version is recorded.
model-update-loophole.fix: Define change triggers by measurable effects, count cumulative changes, and require notice of every change.
model-update-loophole.ex_ai: If minor updates do not require new review, a system can change substantially over time without fresh evaluation.
model-update-loophole.ex_other: For illustration: a bill approving a drug formulation could require new review only for a major change, so many small ingredient swaps might never be reviewed together.

loading-sequence.name: Order of obligations
loading-sequence.plain: Putting some duties first and the stronger ones later gives time to shape the later rules while the real consequences arrive last.
loading-sequence.check: List every duty with its start date. Ask which duties carry the most weight and when they begin, and whether early easy duties could be treated as full compliance.
loading-sequence.fix: Start the most consequential duties early or tie later phases to fixed dates.
loading-sequence.ex_ai: Putting disclosure duties first and safety standards later gives time to influence the later rules while the consequences come last.
loading-sequence.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on bank capital might start with reporting duties now and leave the actual capital requirement to a later rule.

transition-speed-mismatch.name: Timelines slower than the change
transition-speed-mismatch.plain: Multi-year timelines for support or compliance can lag changes that happen within months, leaving affected people without help.
transition-speed-mismatch.check: Compare each timeline for support, compliance or review with how fast the underlying change can occur. Ask what happens to affected people during the gap.
transition-speed-mismatch.fix: Match timelines to the pace of change and add interim support.
transition-speed-mismatch.ex_ai: Multi-year timelines for support or compliance can lag changes that happen within months, leaving affected people without help.
transition-speed-mismatch.ex_other: For illustration: a bill funding retraining for plant closures over a five year ramp could leave workers without help in the first year.

rolling-emergency-authorization.name: Emergency authority without an end
rolling-emergency-authorization.plain: Emergency approvals with no end date or later compliance requirement can let a product or practice become entrenched.
rolling-emergency-authorization.check: Find each emergency or temporary authority. Ask who declares it, what ends it, whether it can be renewed without limit, and whether the thing authorized must later meet normal standards.
rolling-emergency-authorization.fix: Set an end date, limit renewals, and require normal standards after a stated period.
rolling-emergency-authorization.ex_ai: Emergency approvals with no end date or compliance requirement allow systems to become entrenched.
rolling-emergency-authorization.ex_other: For illustration: a bill allowing emergency use of a water treatment method could let it run for years with no later safety review.

national-security-carveout.name: Security carve-out
national-security-carveout.plain: Broad exemptions or waivers for security can be defined widely enough to cover uses that are routine rather than urgent.
national-security-carveout.check: Find each security or defense exemption. Ask how the term is defined, who decides it applies, whether there is oversight or reporting, and what ordinary activities could fit inside it.
national-security-carveout.fix: Define the exemption narrowly by purpose, require written findings, and add oversight reporting.
national-security-carveout.ex_ai: Broad exemptions or waivers for national security can be defined widely enough to cover surveillance, policing and border uses.
national-security-carveout.ex_other: For illustration: a data privacy bill might exempt any processing for security purposes, which could cover routine customer tracking.

trade-secret-exemption.name: Trade secret exemptions
trade-secret-exemption.plain: Trade secret protection can limit disclosure to high-level descriptions, withholding the detail needed for independent checking.
trade-secret-exemption.check: Find every confidentiality or proprietary carve-out from disclosure. Ask who decides what is secret, whether regulators and vetted outside reviewers can still see it, and what is published.
trade-secret-exemption.fix: Allow regulator and vetted reviewer access to protected material, with limited public summaries.
trade-secret-exemption.ex_ai: Trade secret protection can limit disclosure to high-level descriptions, withholding detail needed for independent evaluation.
trade-secret-exemption.ex_other: For illustration: a food labeling bill could protect recipes as trade secrets in a way that also withholds the amounts of allergens.

open-source-definition.name: Exemption defined by distribution method
open-source-definition.plain: How an exemption defines the way a product is distributed decides whether it covers genuinely community projects or large firms releasing parts of their products.
open-source-definition.check: Find any exemption based on how something is shared or licensed. Ask how the term is defined, who benefits, and whether a large firm could qualify by releasing only part.
open-source-definition.fix: Define the exemption by who controls and profits from the product, not only by license terms.
open-source-definition.ex_ai: How open source is defined decides whether an exemption covers genuinely open projects or large companies releasing parts of their models.
open-source-definition.ex_other: For illustration: a bill exempting freely distributed software tools could cover a large vendor that gives away a basic version and charges for the rest.

parental-responsibility.name: Offering a control as safe harbor
parental-responsibility.plain: Offering a user-side control, such as a parental setting, can be treated as meeting the duty, shifting responsibility to people who may lack the knowledge or time to use it.
parental-responsibility.check: Find any provision that treats offering a tool, notice or consent mechanism as satisfying a duty. Ask whether people realistically use it, and whether the default is protective.
parental-responsibility.fix: Set protective defaults and measure whether the control is used, not only offered.
parental-responsibility.ex_ai: Offering parental controls can be treated as meeting the duty, shifting responsibility to parents who may lack technical knowledge.
parental-responsibility.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on online gambling could count a spending limit setting as compliance, even if few users ever turn it on.

synthetic-data-escape.name: Derived data treated as out of scope
synthetic-data-escape.plain: Data produced from personal information may be treated as outside privacy rules even though it can carry information about individuals.
synthetic-data-escape.check: Find terms like anonymized, de-identified, aggregated or derived data. Ask what test decides this, who applies it, whether re-identification is possible, and whether the rules still apply if it is.
synthetic-data-escape.fix: Use a tested standard for identifiability and keep protections if re-identification becomes possible.
synthetic-data-escape.ex_ai: Data generated from personal data may be treated as outside privacy rules, even though it carries information derived from individuals.
synthetic-data-escape.ex_other: For illustration: a health records bill could exempt aggregated data sets, even when small groups make individual patients identifiable.

manipulation-definition.name: Intent required to count as harmful influence
manipulation-definition.plain: Requiring deceptive intent or coercion before conduct counts as improper influence can leave out designs that exploit people without any such intent.
manipulation-definition.check: Find the mental state or method a definition requires. Ask whether conduct with the same effect but no proven intent would be covered, and who must prove intent.
manipulation-definition.fix: Define the covered conduct by its effect on people as well as by intent.
manipulation-definition.ex_ai: Requiring deceptive intent or coercion before something counts as manipulation leaves out engagement design that exploits users without such intent.
manipulation-definition.ex_other: For illustration: a consumer bill banning deceptive sales tactics might not reach a checkout flow built to exploit habit, if no one intended to deceive.

synthetic-content-definition.name: Definition requiring wholly one category
synthetic-content-definition.plain: Requiring something to be entirely of one kind before a rule applies leaves out mixed items, where a person edited or combined it with other material.
synthetic-content-definition.check: Find definitions that require a thing to be wholly, entirely or solely of a type. Ask what happens to mixtures and edited items, and whether a small change would take them outside the rule.
synthetic-content-definition.fix: Cover items that are wholly or partly of the type, with a test for how much counts.
synthetic-content-definition.ex_ai: Requiring content to be entirely AI-generated leaves out mixed content that a person edited from an AI draft.
synthetic-content-definition.ex_other: For illustration: a food labeling bill covering products that are entirely imported could miss goods blended with a small share of local material.

vulnerable-populations-definition.name: Narrow list of protected groups
vulnerable-populations-definition.plain: A narrow list of protected groups can leave out people who are vulnerable in practice, such as minors, people in crisis or those under economic pressure.
vulnerable-populations-definition.check: Find any list of protected people or groups. Ask who is missing, whether the list is closed, and whether a situational test could cover people vulnerable at a given time.
vulnerable-populations-definition.fix: Use an open list or a functional test of vulnerability alongside named groups.
vulnerable-populations-definition.ex_ai: A narrow list of vulnerable groups can leave out minors, people with cognitive decline, people in crisis and the economically desperate.
vulnerable-populations-definition.ex_other: For illustration: a lending bill protecting named groups from abusive terms could miss borrowers in sudden financial distress.

risk-framework-definition.name: Risk categories set narrowly
risk-framework-definition.plain: Risk categories focused on one kind of harm, such as physical safety, can leave out others such as economic disruption, loss of rights or concentration of power.
risk-framework-definition.check: Find the categories or tiers that decide which duties apply. Ask which harms they cover, which they leave out, and who can add or change categories.
risk-framework-definition.fix: List the harms to be considered, including slow and social ones, and let categories be revised.
risk-framework-definition.ex_ai: Risk categories focused on physical safety leave out risks such as labor disruption, democratic erosion and concentration of power.
risk-framework-definition.ex_other: For illustration: a transport bill sorting vehicles by crash risk might ignore harms such as data collection or market lock-in.

no-structural-remedies.name: Remedies limited to money
no-structural-remedies.plain: Excluding court power to order changes to a product or practice, or to order divestiture, can limit remedies to money payments that may be treated as a cost of business.
no-structural-remedies.check: Find the remedies a court or agency may order. Ask whether they can require changes to conduct, design or ownership, or only fines and damages, and whether fines are large enough to matter.
no-structural-remedies.fix: Authorize injunctions and structural relief in addition to monetary penalties.
no-structural-remedies.ex_ai: Excluding court power to order changes to algorithms or divestiture of data limits remedies to money.
no-structural-remedies.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on market concentration could allow fines but bar courts from ordering a firm to sell a business line.

penalties-flat.name: Flat penalties that shrink with scale
penalties-flat.plain: Flat per-violation penalties can be small relative to a large firm's earnings, while revenue-based penalties scale with size.
penalties-flat.check: Find each penalty amount. Ask whether it is fixed or scales with revenue, harm or gain, and compare it to what a large actor earns from the conduct.
penalties-flat.fix: Set penalties as the greater of a fixed sum or a share of revenue or gain.
penalties-flat.ex_ai: Flat per-violation penalties are small for large companies, while revenue-based penalties scale with size.
penalties-flat.ex_other: For illustration: a bill setting a fixed fine per day for emissions could be less than the cost of installing controls at a large plant.

limitations-period.name: Short limitations period
limitations-period.plain: A short filing period can close the window before many harms are discovered, especially harms that appear slowly.
limitations-period.check: Find each deadline for bringing a claim. Ask when the clock starts, whether it runs from the act or from discovery, and how long the harm typically takes to appear.
cues: after the date of the violation
limitations-period.fix: Start the clock at discovery and allow extra time for harms that appear late.
limitations-period.ex_ai: A short filing period can close the window before many harms are discovered.
limitations-period.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on workplace exposure could allow claims for one year after the exposure, though illness may appear decades later.

tax-treatment.name: Tax treatment that rewards the activity
tax-treatment.plain: Tax rules such as accelerated depreciation and credits can make an activity profitable regardless of its wider effects, working against the goals of other provisions.
tax-treatment.check: Find tax credits, deductions and write-offs. Ask which activities they reward, whether they conflict with the law's other goals, and whether they carry conditions tied to those goals.
tax-treatment.fix: Tie tax benefits to conditions that match the law's stated goals.
tax-treatment.ex_ai: Tax rules such as accelerated depreciation and credits make deployment profitable regardless of social effects.
tax-treatment.ex_other: For illustration: a bill promoting warehouse automation could give rapid write-offs for equipment that cut the jobs another section tries to protect.

productivity-gains.name: Gains go to owners
productivity-gains.plain: With no mechanism for sharing gains from a change, benefits can accrue to owners, and funds meant to spread them can be described as a penalty on progress.
productivity-gains.check: Find who receives the gains from the activity the law promotes and who bears the costs. Ask whether any fund, fee or sharing rule connects the two.
productivity-gains.fix: Add a funding source or sharing rule that directs part of the gains to those who bear the costs.
productivity-gains.ex_ai: With no mechanism for sharing productivity gains, benefits accrue to owners, and transition funds can be described as penalizing innovation.
productivity-gains.ex_other: For illustration: a bill speeding approval of a new port could leave all revenue with the operator and none for nearby residents who bear the traffic.

stakeholder-process.name: Stakeholder process design
stakeholder-process.plain: Consensus requirements in stakeholder processes can give a veto to the best organized participants, and expertise weighting or short timelines can sideline others.
stakeholder-process.check: Find any advisory or standard-setting group. Ask who sits on it, how it decides, whether consensus gives a veto, how long it has, and whether the agency may depart from its output.
stakeholder-process.fix: Set balanced membership, majority or reasoned decisions, adequate time and agency authority to decide.
stakeholder-process.ex_ai: Consensus requirements in stakeholder processes give a veto to industry, and expertise weighting or short timelines can marginalize civil society.
stakeholder-process.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on telecom standards could require consensus of a working group, so any single large member can block a rule.

technical-capacity-limits.name: Limits on regulator capacity
technical-capacity-limits.plain: Barring internal testing tools, requiring reliance on outside assessors, or setting low pay scales can reduce a regulator's own ability to evaluate.
technical-capacity-limits.check: Find limits on the regulator's staffing, tools, pay and contracting. Ask whether it can test or investigate by itself, or must rely on the regulated party or paid third parties.
technical-capacity-limits.fix: Authorize the regulator to build its own testing capacity and set competitive pay.
technical-capacity-limits.ex_ai: Barring internal testing tools, requiring third-party assessments or low pay scales reduces the regulator's own ability to evaluate.
technical-capacity-limits.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on building inspections could require agencies to accept private inspector reports and bar them from buying testing equipment.

transparency-defined-down.name: Transparency defined thinly
transparency-defined-down.plain: A bare notice that something exists or applies is less informative than disclosing how it works and its limits, and a law can require only the former.
transparency-defined-down.check: Find what exactly must be disclosed and to whom. Ask whether the disclosure lets a reader judge quality, risks and limits, or only confirms that a thing exists.
transparency-defined-down.fix: Specify the content of disclosures, including limits and known risks, and who receives them.
transparency-defined-down.ex_ai: A bare statement that content is AI-generated is less informative than disclosing training data and limitations, and laws can require only the former.
transparency-defined-down.ex_other: For illustration: a financial product bill could require a notice that fees apply without listing the amounts or when they are charged.

labeling-reductionism.name: Labeling treated as the whole solution
labeling-reductionism.plain: Labeling is inexpensive and may have little effect on what people believe or do, but can be treated as sufficient in place of structural measures.
labeling-reductionism.check: Find where a label, notice or watermark is the only duty. Ask what evidence shows it changes behavior and what happens when it is ignored, removed or unseen.
labeling-reductionism.fix: Pair labels with substantive duties and test whether the labels work.
labeling-reductionism.ex_ai: Labeling is inexpensive and may have little effect on belief, but can be treated as sufficient in place of structural measures.
labeling-reductionism.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on sugary drinks might require only a warning label and no limit on marketing to children.

researcher-access.name: Researcher and journalist access
researcher-access.plain: Without statutory access rights, independent study of an industry depends on company goodwill, which can be withdrawn.
researcher-access.check: Check whether outside researchers, auditors and journalists have a legal right to data or facilities. Ask who qualifies, who can refuse, and whether good-faith research is protected from legal threats.
researcher-access.fix: Create a legal access right for vetted researchers, with safe harbor for good-faith work.
researcher-access.ex_ai: Without statutory access rights, independent evaluation depends on company goodwill that can be withdrawn.
researcher-access.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on hospital pricing could require posting prices but give researchers no right to the underlying billing data.

whistleblower-absence.name: Missing whistleblower protection
whistleblower-absence.plain: Employees are a likely source of information about problems, and without legal protection they can be silenced or penalized for speaking.
whistleblower-absence.check: Check whether the law protects people who report violations, including from retaliation, and whether it provides a safe channel. Ask who is covered, what remedy exists and who enforces it.
whistleblower-absence.fix: Add anti-retaliation protection, confidential reporting channels and a remedy for retaliation.
whistleblower-absence.ex_ai: Employees are a likely source of safety information, and without protection they can be silenced or penalized.
whistleblower-absence.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on food plant safety might create inspection duties but offer no protection for workers who report violations.

nda-enforceability.name: Confidentiality agreements limit reporting
nda-enforceability.plain: If nondisclosure agreements stay fully enforceable, or exceptions apply only to confidential official channels, people may be unable to report concerns.
nda-enforceability.check: Find how the law treats confidentiality agreements. Ask whether they can block reports to regulators or the public, and whether the exception covers more than one confidential channel.
nda-enforceability.fix: Void agreement terms that bar lawful reporting and allow reports to regulators and others.
nda-enforceability.ex_ai: If nondisclosure agreements stay fully enforceable, or exceptions apply only to confidential regulatory channels, employees may be unable to report safety concerns.
nda-enforceability.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on nursing home care might protect reports to the state agency but leave non-disparagement clauses enforceable against talking to families.

training-data-provenance.name: No records of input origin
training-data-provenance.plain: Without requirements to record where inputs came from, material of uncertain origin cannot be traced and its quality or legality stays unaccountable.
training-data-provenance.check: Check whether the law requires records of the source of inputs, materials or data. Ask who keeps them, how long, and who can inspect them.
training-data-provenance.fix: Require origin records for inputs, with retention periods and inspection rights.
training-data-provenance.ex_ai: Without provenance requirements, training data of uncertain origin cannot be traced and inputs stay unaccountable.
training-data-provenance.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on imported seafood could set quality rules but not require records of where the catch originated.

retention-deletion-tension.name: Retention versus deletion tension
retention-deletion-tension.plain: The tension between keeping records for accountability and deleting data for privacy can be invoked either way depending on convenience.
retention-deletion-tension.check: Find duties to keep records and duties to delete data. Ask which prevails when they conflict, who decides, and whether a retention period is stated.
retention-deletion-tension.fix: State which duty prevails in each case and set retention periods with exceptions for audits.
retention-deletion-tension.ex_ai: The tension between keeping records for accountability and deleting data for privacy can be invoked either way depending on convenience.
retention-deletion-tension.ex_other: For illustration: a bill requiring both audit logs and prompt deletion of customer data might let a firm cite either to avoid producing records.

reported-vs-published.name: Reported but not published
reported-vs-published.plain: Reports sent to regulators without public release prevent public pressure and comparison between firms.
reported-vs-published.check: Find each reporting duty and who receives the report. Ask whether it is published, in what form, how soon, and who may keep it confidential.
reported-vs-published.fix: Require public release of reports in summary or redacted form, with narrow confidentiality grounds.
reported-vs-published.ex_ai: Reports sent to regulators without public release prevent public pressure and comparison.
reported-vs-published.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on school safety incidents might require reports to a state office but exempt them from public records requests.

reporting-frequency-lag.name: Reporting too infrequent
reporting-frequency-lag.plain: Annual reporting for things that change quickly means the information is always out of date by the time it is seen.
reporting-frequency-lag.check: Find how often reports are due and how long after the period they are published. Ask how fast the subject changes and whether serious events must be reported sooner.
reporting-frequency-lag.fix: Set report frequency to the pace of change and add prompt notice of serious events.
reporting-frequency-lag.ex_ai: Annual reporting for systems that change weekly means information is always outdated.
reporting-frequency-lag.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on wildfire risk equipment might require a yearly report though conditions change within days.

section-230-interaction.name: Interaction with an existing liability shield
section-230-interaction.plain: Whether a new activity counts as publishing or neutral hosting under an existing immunity can be unresolved, and the bill may be silent on it.
section-230-interaction.check: Find any existing law that shields a class of actors from liability. Ask whether the bill says if it applies to the new activity, and who decides if the text is silent.
section-230-interaction.fix: State whether the existing shield applies to the new conduct and, if so, with what limits.
section-230-interaction.ex_ai: Whether algorithmic curation counts as publishing or neutral hosting is unresolved, and the bill may be silent on it.
section-230-interaction.ex_other: For illustration: a bill creating duties for ride platforms might not say whether an older liability shield for intermediaries still applies.

ip-laundering.name: Output as original work (AI outputs)
ip-laundering.check: Find how the bill treats ownership of machine-generated output and the use of existing works as input. Ask whether the people whose works were used have any claim or notice.
ip-laundering.ex_ai: Treating AI outputs as original works can reduce the leverage of rights holders over the use of their work for training.

preempting-anti-discrimination.name: Narrow standard displaces stronger law
preempting-anti-discrimination.plain: A new, weaker standard on a topic can displace stronger claims under existing civil rights or consumer laws if the text is not clear about overlap.
preempting-anti-discrimination.check: Find preemption, supremacy and savings language. Ask whether existing rights and remedies survive, and whether compliance with the new law is treated as compliance with older ones.
preempting-anti-discrimination.fix: State that existing rights and remedies remain, and that compliance here does not excuse compliance elsewhere.
preempting-anti-discrimination.ex_ai: Weaker AI-specific standards may displace stronger claims under existing civil rights laws.
preempting-anti-discrimination.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on tenant screening could set a mild fairness test and be read to replace stronger claims under housing law.

takings-traps.name: Takings exposure
takings-traps.plain: Provisions that compel sharing or access to property can draw takings challenges that could limit regulation of whole categories.
takings-traps.check: Find any duty that forces a party to share, license or give access to assets. Ask whether compensation is addressed and whether a challenge could strike the broader scheme.
takings-traps.fix: Provide compensation or narrow the compelled access, and include fallback provisions if challenged.
takings-traps.ex_ai: Data sharing or forced access provisions can draw takings challenges that could limit regulation of whole categories.
takings-traps.ex_other: For illustration: a bill forcing utilities to open private lines to competitors could be challenged for lack of compensation.

voluntary-commitments.name: Voluntary commitments as substitute
voluntary-commitments.plain: Voluntary pledges cited as proof that law is unnecessary can later be written into the law as its standard, fixing a low bar.
voluntary-commitments.check: Find references to voluntary frameworks, pledges or best practices. Ask whether the law adopts them as its standard, who wrote them, and whether they are enforceable.
voluntary-commitments.fix: Set the standard in the statute, with voluntary measures only as a floor.
voluntary-commitments.ex_ai: Voluntary pledges cited as proof that law is unnecessary can later be written into the law as its standard.
voluntary-commitments.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on data brokers might adopt an industry code of conduct as the legal safe harbor.

tool-not-agent.name: Characterization that assigns responsibility
tool-not-agent.plain: Describing a product as a mere tool, or by another label, can limit the responsibility of its maker and block rules suited to how it actually behaves.
tool-not-agent.check: Find labels that describe what a thing is, such as tool, aid or assistant. Ask what legal consequences follow from the label, and whether the actual behavior fits.
tool-not-agent.fix: Attach duties to function and effect rather than to a descriptive label.
tool-not-agent.ex_ai: Describing AI as a tool can limit responsibility and block rules suited to autonomous systems.
tool-not-agent.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on automated trading might call software a mere tool of the trader, so the maker faces no duty when it acts unexpectedly.

procurement-standards.name: Government purchasing as standard-setting
procurement-standards.plain: Public purchasing rules can effectively set industry standards with little public scrutiny and can favor incumbents.
procurement-standards.check: Find rules on government purchasing, contracts or acquisition that set requirements. Ask who writes them, whether the public can comment, and whether they favor firms already in the market.
procurement-standards.fix: Open purchasing standards to public comment and set them to match the law's goals.
procurement-standards.ex_ai: Federal procurement rules effectively set industry standards with little public scrutiny and can favor incumbents.
procurement-standards.ex_other: For illustration: a bill on school technology could set purchasing requirements that only large vendors can meet.

vertical-integration.name: Rules on one layer favor integrated firms
vertical-integration.plain: Rules applying to one layer of a supply chain favor firms that span several layers and can shift costs between them.
vertical-integration.check: Map the layers of the industry and see which the rules cover. Ask whether a firm operating in several layers can move costs or activity to an uncovered one.
vertical-integration.fix: Apply rules to the integrated firm as a whole or add rules on dealings between its units.
vertical-integration.ex_ai: Rules applying to one layer favor integrated firms that can shift costs between layers.
vertical-integration.ex_other: For illustration: a bill capping fees by pharmacies might not cover a firm that owns both the insurer and the pharmacy.

starving-the-regulator.ex_ai: Limiting a regulator's technical expertise through funding and staffing can make enforcement look ineffective.

strategic-complexity.name: Complexity that hides the operative rule
strategic-complexity.plain: Text so long, layered or cross-referenced that few readers can find what it does can let a significant provision pass without scrutiny.
strategic-complexity.check: Count the cross-references and nested exceptions a reader must follow to learn what one provision does. Ask whether the operative rule could be stated in one place.
strategic-complexity.fix: State each operative rule in one place, limit nested cross-references, and supply a section-by-section summary that matches the text.
strategic-complexity.ex_ai: Submitting thousands of pages of technical documentation can obscure information through volume.
strategic-complexity.ex_other: For illustration: a benefits bill whose eligibility rule can only be found by reading four sections and two other statutes together.
